passages.text: Pollination, and more specifically insect pollinators, are essential to healthy ecosystems and play a critical role in both crop production and the reproduction of many flowering plant species. Nearly 70% of leading crop species experience increased production when pollinators are present [1]. The European honeybee (Apis mellifera) often receives the most attention and recognition as a pollinator. However, A. mellifera is only one of over 20,000 species of bee documented worldwide [2]. In contrast, other species, such as bumble bees, mining bees, mason bees, and leafcutter bees, are under-studied and under-appreciated despite evidence that native pollinators such as these are more effective than honey bees at pollinating a number of flowering crop species [3–5]. Native solitary bees such as Osmia lignaria have even been developed as managed crop pollinators in North America [6,7]. These bees also exhibit a diverse array of life histories, ecological niches, and nesting habits. The majority (roughly 90%) of bee species are solitary [8] and build nests in soil (ground nesters) or dead wood, stems, or piles of brush (cavity nesters) [9]. While some native bees are generalists, gathering resources from a wide array of flowering plant species, some are specialists, and will only collect pollen from a select few species [9]. This intricate dependence on specific plant species and habitat structures makes native pollinators vulnerable to habitat loss and human disturbance [9].

One increasingly popular tool to help mitigate these problems for native pollinators is the pollinator hotel. While the majority of solitary bee species are ground nesters (approximately 70%), pollinator hotels can serve as habitat for the remaining 30% of cavity nesting species [10]. These structures are also commonly called bee hotels, but they often host a variety of solitary wasps as well as cavity-nesting bees [11]. Mason bees (Osmia spp.) and leafcutter bees (Megachile spp.) are the two most common genera reported utilizing pollinator hotels [11]. Mason wasps (Vespidae: Eumeninae), grass carrying wasps (Isodontia spp.), and square-headed wasps (Crabronidae) are also frequently observed inhabiting the hotels [9]. While bee species provide valuable pollination services, solitary wasps found in pollinator hotels also contribute to controlling pest insect populations [12].

Pollinator hotels replicate cavity nesting species’ natural nesting sites by offering access to hollow tubes, often made of bamboo, reeds, cardboard, drilled wooden blocks, or the stems of native plants [9]. Providing the bees with a diverse array of materials may help to attract a wider range of bee species [14]. However, each material type has its own unique attractants and drawbacks. Drilled blocks, for example, are known to be extremely attractive to both bee and wasp species but are difficult to maintain [15]. Any old nests left in the blocks may contain diseases or parasites that are impossible to completely remove. Likewise, positioning the drilled holes too near to the edges of the block can make the nests susceptible to parasitism, especially by the Leucospis affinis wasp [16]. Bamboo or reed tubes with too large a diameter may be either left completely unoccupied or preferentially host large non-native bees such as the aggressive giant resin bee (Megachile sculpturalis) [14]. Cardboard tubes are commonly available in commercial nest kits, but very high rates of parasitism have been reported [17].

Regular maintenance is also essential. Many pollinator hotel maintenance practices have extensive anecdotal evidence, but are not backed by empirical data. For example, emergence boxes are small, mostly enclosed containers in which nest materials can be placed to provide a transitional area where the bees can emerge [9]. The old nesting materials can then be removed and cleaned over the winter while the bees are inactive. In the summer, the bees emerge and are free to make nests in fresh materials in the main hotel. These boxes often come with commercial pollinator hotel kits, but there is little to no empirical evidence that demonstrates whether the boxes are an effective tool for pollinator hotel maintenance. There are risks that creating an even greater concentration of nest sites within the emergence boxes can encourage parasitism, or that the emerging insects will return to nest in the boxes rather than the newly-cleaned hotels. This lack of data matters because cleaning pollinator hotels is an essential maintenance task. Chalkbrood and parasitic mites can linger in old nests and spread throughout the pollinator hotel without regular cleaning [17]. Other parasites, such as Houdini flies, beetle larvae, and parasitoid wasps may also accumulate in pollinator hotels without regular maintenance [17].

Parasitic and parasitoid wasps are a common secondary inhabitant of pollinator hotels [9,17,22,23]. The most common of these are Monodontomerus species (Torymidae), L. affinis (Leucospidae), and members of the family Chrysididae. Monodontomerus wasps are tiny parasitoids that lay their eggs in Osmia and Megachile nests [17]. Leucospis affinis also parasitizes the larvae of Osmia and Megachile, along with some species of solitary wasps [22]. Members of the Chrysididae family are common kleptoparasites of several pollinator hotel residents [24,25]. There is some indication that parasitism may be more common in pollinator hotels than in dispersed nesting sites, and that this increase may correlate with the higher density of nest sites that pollinator hotels encourage [13,26,27]. Parasitism in pollinator hotels can disproportionately affect the native bee residents of the hotel, rather than introduced bees or either native or introduced wasp species [13]. If left completely unmanaged, pollinator hotels may become more of a liability to their native, solitary inhabitants [13]. To be effective tools, pollinator hotels must be installed and maintained on a regular schedule, using tools to both preserve the native bee populations and reduce the burden of parasites and parasitoids.

In this study, we investigated the parasite burden present in four pollinator hotels. We also conducted the first empirical study on whether emergence boxes could be implemented as an effective maintenance and cleaning tool. We first conducted a biodiversity study of a single pollinator hotel in North Carolina to understand inhabitant profiles. Secondly, we surveyed the parasite burden across four pollinator hotels. We hypothesized that the parasite burden would be highest in cardboard nest tubes as previously described, but that nests made of reeds would also have a higher parasite load than bamboo tubes because of the relative thinness of the reed tube walls. Lastly, we tested the efficacy of emergence boxes as a maintenance tool. Specifically, we evaluated whether nests placed in emergence boxes would accumulate futher parasitism and whether bees and wasps would construct new nests inside the old materials in the boxes. In half of the emergence boxes, we implemented a one-way valve that we hypothesized would further reduce the rate of bees re-entering the emergence boxes.

The results of the biodiversity survey (Study 1) show that the UNC Asheville pollinator hotel is home to a wide variety of bee and wasp species, but that diversity is unevenly distributed across the hotel. The numbers of observed insects were distributed unevenly throughout the twelve sub-boxes in the hotel as indicated by a chi-square test of independence, but there were no trends across rows or columns of sub-boxes. Additionally, there were no significant differences in the number of families across different areas of the hotel. This was an unexpected result because the upper row of the hotel (sub-boxes 1-4) are shaded by the roof for several hours after the bottom rows have begun to receive sun. Orienting pollinator hotels towards the southeast is standard practice in North America and Europe, and nests with exposure to the morning sun are thought to be more attractive to bees [16], but in our study, the differences in sun exposure appeared to have little affect on overall trends in insect or family abundance.

These results also indicate that parasites are indeed very common in the pollinator hotel. Several of the material types surveyed in Study 1, including paper tubes and bamboo, had nearly the same number of parasitoid insects as non-parasitoid insects found inside. Previous research has found that paper tubes are particularly vulnerable to parasitoids, especially the parasitic wasp Monodontomerus obscurus [17]. Beyond parasitic wasps, birds and rodents have also been observed dismantling bee nests housed in paper tubes, consuming the larvae, and using the paper itself for their own nests [17]. Bamboo and reeds have previously been considered safer for bees, and the thicker walls of these materials can offer some protection from other common parasites like Leucospis affinis [16]. However, the high presence of parasitoids in these materials in the biodiversity survey indicates an underlying problem. Before the start of this research in 2022, the UNC Asheville pollinator hotel had not been properly maintained or cleaned since its construction in 2016. Regular maintenance is necessary to prevent the buildup of parasites and diseases in pollinator hotels [9], and the absence of this maintenance likely explains the large number of parasites observed. These results, while striking, likely overestimate the number of parasitoid insects present in the pollinator hotel, as only adult insects were included in the data set. Unparasitized cocoons containing healthy larvae were therefore likely present but not counted. Nevertheless, the high prevalence of parasites was corroborated in Study 2, where insects were reared from nests rather than relying on a snapshot of adult presence.

The four families of parasites represented in Study 2 differed from those documented in the first study. Ichnumonid and Eulophid wasps were not documented in the first study at all (likely due to small size in the case of the Eulophids), while significant levels of L. affinis wasps and chrysidid were observed that were not then documented in the second study. Leucospid and chrysidid wasps were observed again in the emergence box study (Study 3), though in low numbers (one individual each). The discrepancies in the identified families between the three studies could be due in part to the sampling method. It could also be due to the confluence of factors contributing to nesting success – flight range, proximity and co-occurrence of resources, and other factors. The second study used only nests made in new, undamaged nest materials that had only been in the pollinator hotel for two months. It is possible that leucospids and chrysidids are more prone to parasitizing damaged materials, or that the positioning of the new tubes in tight bundles made it more difficult for the wasps to penetrate them. Leucospid wasps, specifically, rely on ovipositors to penetrate up to 3/4 of an inch into the outside of a nest to reach the bee’s cocoon [16]. The materials located towards the inside of our material bundles would likely have been inaccessible to the wasps, which may have influenced the types of parasites seen in the study.

The patterns of parasite burden observed across the eulophid and torymid species were more expected. The far higher abundance of parasites observed in paper tubes as compared to bamboo and reeds fits both with our hypotheses and with previous research that paper tubes are more susceptible to parasitism [17]. Eulophid wasps were also more common in bamboo nests than reed ones. However, as there was no significant difference between the levels of Torymid wasps present in reeds versus bamboo, we are unable to fully support our original hypothesis that reeds are more susceptible to parasitism than bamboo. The susceptibility of bamboo to parasitoids in general is much less well studied than the susceptibility of paper tubes. Further, we are prevented from making determinations about the reasons behind the greater burden of eulophid wasps in bamboo tubes by the obscure nature of the wasp itself. The species of wasp observed at the pollinator hotel was identified as belonging to the family Eulophidae, genus Melittobia, by the Plant Disease and Insect Clinic (NC State University). However, the species was unable to be determined, and the life history and host(s) of this wasp are unknown. Future research should also include the effects of diameter as a covariate factor that may affect overall parasite abundance in addition to material type.

The patterns of parasite burden across the four pollinator hotel locations were less expected. Torymid and eulophid parasites displayed nearly opposite trends. The levels of eulophid parasites were orders of magnitude lower in the three NC State hotels than the UNC Asheville hotel. Torymid wasps (specifically Monodontomerus obscurus) which occurred in significantly greater numbers in all three NC State pollinator hotels, are known parasitoids of Osmia and Megachile bees [17]. Parasitoid wasps have been suggested to be especially susceptible to host competition because of their reliance on limited hosts to complete their reproductive cycles [47]. While both M. obscurus and many wasps in the eulophid genus Melittobia are generalists, and thus able to parasitize a variety of host species [48–50], the limited number of hosts within the pollinator hotel may still lead to interspecific competition. Additionally, since the hosts are more concentrated in the pollinator hotel than they would usually be in the wild, the wasps may have reduced barriers to finding hosts [47]. Many species of wasps have been shown to co-parasitize the same larva, even if only one species can ultimately develop [51]. If the torymid and eulophid wasps were engaging in co-parasitism or subjected to increased interspecific competition due to the increased population density of the pollinator hotel environment, competitive exclusion of torymids by the eulophids may have occured at the UNC Asheville hotel.

One of the primary concerns with emergence boxes as a tool to reduce parasite burden was the risk of confining healthy, unparasitized nest cells in the same small space as parasitized cocoons. Because parasitoids such as Monodontomerus have shorter generation times than their hosts, they can multiply greatly over a single season in a bee hotel or emergence box. If the parasitoids were able to hatch before most of the bees, the box itself might serve as an accelerator of parasitism, since it increases population density even more than in the hotels itself. The increased population density of pollinator hotels has been previously linked to increased risk of parasitism [26]. However, small numbers of new parasitoid holes were observed across all three treatments at the end of the emergence box study, which indicates that parasitoid wasps did not eclose and parasitize bee cocoons before the bees themselves were able to leave the boxes. While some nest tubes did increase parasitoid holes over the study, the data were heavily skewed towards zero levels, indicating that additional parasitism inside the emergence boxes was uncommon. This bodes well for the success of emergence boxes as a maintenance tool.

The other main concern with emergence boxes is the potential for bees to re-nest inside them. While an emergence box is in use, the rest of the materials in the hotel can be cleaned and replaced as needed to reduce the buildup of parasitoid wasps, mites, and fungal pathogens [9]. Cavity-nesting bees seek protected cavities to nest in, and, if the bee has just emerged from an emergence box, it may decide to return to the box to make its new nest. In the third study, while the proportion of bees that re-nested in the emergence box was not zero, it was low (at or below 12.5% when mud type changes are included, at or below 4.6% when mud type changes are not included) across all three treatments. This indicates that the great majority of bees that hatch out of the emergence boxes found another area (presumably the cleaned and refreshed pollinator hotel nearby) to make their nests in. Most of these re-nesting events consisted of transitions between different types of mud caps, rather than transitions from resin, leaf pulp, or grass. This indicates that mason bees, rather than leafcutter bees, resin bees, or grass wasps, likely return to nest in the emergence boxes most frequently. However, because the mud color changes could potentially be due to environmental effects and because every type of material underwent at least one re-nesting event, no definitive conclusions can be drawn about which families of bees are most likely to re-nest in an emergence box. Additionally, because insects were identified only to the family level and because of the relatively small number of nest materials that were reared out in the lab, we were unable to make concrete connections between particular groups of bees and their relative likelihood to re-nest in the emergence boxes. Insects were unable to be further identified to genera and/or species due to the damage samples sustained while in storage from sustained power outages associated with Hurricane Helene.

Taken together, the results of these three studies highlight both the ecological complexity and management challenges of artificial nesting habitats for solitary bees. Patterns of biodiversity and parasitism at the UNC Asheville pollinator hotel reveal how environmental orientation, maintenance history, and material choice shape community composition and parasite load. The differences in parasitoid prevalence and family across the four hotel locations underscore the strong influence of site-specific factors and potential interactions among parasitoid species. Finally, the emergence box experiment demonstrates that these tools may allow for pollinator hotel maintenance without significantly increasing parasitism risk or encouraging extensive re-nesting within the emergence boxes themselves. While certain behaviors, such as limited re-nesting, merit further study, the overall findings suggest that careful placement, regular cleaning, and the strategic use of emergence boxes can enhance the long-term health and sustainability of managed pollinator populations.

Our results should be used to improve the maintenance practices for pollinator hotels because of their value not only as conservation tools, but as educational platforms that can shape public understanding of native bee ecology. Pollinator hotels are ideal venues for students, citizen scientists, and the broader community to directly observe species interactions and the consequences of different management decisions. Effective pollinator hotel management contributes to sustaining native bee populations that are integral to the reproduction of both wild and managed flowering plants systems. As habitat loss and anthropogenic pressures continue to threaten pollinator communities globally, initiatives that integrate research, maintenance, and public education can help foster ecological literacy while directly supporting pollinator preservation. In this way, well-managed pollinator hotels can function not only as nesting habitat but as living classrooms that connect local conservation actions to global concerns about biodiversity, ecosystem resilience, and our agricultural system.

passages.text: The levels of phenotypic variability observed in this study are consistent with those reported in pearl millet diversity panels evaluated across West Africa and the broader semi-arid tropics [12,30], confirming that the Senegalese germplasm captures a representative range of genetic diversity for the traits studied. The high CV for grain yield reflects the phenotypic heterogeneity of the panel entries rather than residual segregation; this heterogeneity is expected given that the panel draws on entries from different breeding sources. The relatively low variation in flowering time compared to yield-related traits follows a pattern widely documented in pearl millet, where photoperiod sensitivity and adaptation to terminal drought impose strong directional selection on phenology while leaving morphological and yield traits more open to diversification [31].

Heritability estimates across traits were consistent with the quantitative genetic architecture expected for pearl millet under Sahelian conditions. The relatively high H2 for grain yield indicates a substantial genetic basis for yield variation in this panel, comparable to values reported from combining ability and multi-environment studies in West African pearl millet [32], though the residual environmental component underscores the importance of multi-environment evaluation for reliable selection gains. The high heritability observed for panicle length and plant height reflects their predominantly additive genetic architecture and lower sensitivity to G × E interaction, consistent with findings across recombinant inbred line populations and diversity panels in pearl millet [33,34]. The moderate to high heritability for flowering time aligns with reports from Senegalese landraces [35], where photoperiod sensitivity introduces trial-to-trial variation while maintaining a meaningful genetic signal. These estimates suggest that direct phenotypic selection will be most efficient for morphological traits, while grain yield improvement will require multi-environment testing and genomic-assisted approaches to effectively capture and exploit the available genetic variation.

The phenotypic distribution across the GWAS panel revealed substantial variation for all four traits, consistent with quantitative inheritance and phenotypic ranges reported in pearl millet panels evaluated across West Africa and the semi-arid tropics [12,30]. The correlation structure reflected biologically meaningful associations consistent with patterns widely documented in pearl millet: the positive relationships among plant height, panicle length, and grain yield suggest shared developmental pathways and pleiotropic genetic control, while the negative correlation between flowering time and grain yield reflects the drought escape mechanism whereby early flowering confers yield stability under terminal drought, a priority selection criterion in Sahelian breeding programs [31]. These patterns support the use of indirect selection through morphological traits under favorable conditions and confirm early flowering as a key target for adaptation to the Senegalese rainfall pattern.

The genetic-diversity indices and the population-structure analysis were computed on complementary subsets rather than on a single panel, and are best read together. Gene diversity, PIC, observed heterozygosity, and inbreeding coefficients were estimated on the full genotyped set (279 genotypes), which still included early-generation segregating material, whereas the PAM/PCA structure analysis was restricted to the 137 advanced, genetically stable entries that formed the association panel. The moderate gene diversity (GD) and PIC observed in both groups are consistent with previous SNP-based characterizations of pearl millet germplasm, where these indices typically range from 0.20 to 0.40 depending on origin, breeding history, and marker density [12,36]. The slightly lower diversity in Group 1 (PMiGAP inbreds) relative to Group 2 reflects the cumulative effect of directional selection within the ICRISAT breeding program, since elite pools under sustained improvement predictably harbour narrower allelic ranges than locally adapted or multi-cross material [37]. Group 2, by contrast, is compositionally heterogeneous: check cultivars alongside multi-cross lines spanning early to advanced generations, and this breadth sustains higher allelic diversity through the accumulated recombination and residual segregation characteristic of early-generation material, accounting for its elevated GD and PIC. These contrasts bear directly on how heterozygosity was interpreted and how the association panel was assembled. The near-identical observed heterozygosity across the two groups is consistent with the allogamous, protogynous reproductive biology of pearl millet, and the moderate inbreeding coefficients confirm that the genotyped diversity set had not reached fixation. Because non-fixed genotypes violate the fixed-line assumption underlying single-marker association testing and can inflate association noise, the early-generation segregating material was excluded and the GWAS was restricted to the 137 stable entries; residual relatedness within that panel was then controlled through a kinship matrix in the mixed-model framework [38,39]. Finally, although the PIC values fall at the lower end of the moderately informative range [40], they remain adequate for association analysis given the large number of markers retained after quality filtering, while the minor-allele-frequency spectrum spans rare variants of potential relevance to adaptation in the Sahelian environment.

Population structure within the 137-entry association panel was weak and largely continuous. PAM clustering identified k = 2 as the silhouette optimum, yet average silhouette widths remained below 0.05 across all values of k, indicating that the panel does not resolve into sharply differentiated subpopulations. This near-continuous stratification is consistent with the panel’s composition, in which PMiGAP lines and local multi-cross material derived from ICRISAT parents share substantial ancestry rather than forming discrete pools. Soft genetic boundaries of this kind are expected in an obligate outcrosser, where protogynous flowering and wind pollination sustain continuous gene flow that prevents sharp discontinuities [41,42]. The low variance captured by individual principal components is likewise a known property of high-dimensional differentiation in outcrossing cereals rather than a shortcoming of the panel, and has been reported for comparable West African germplasm [36,37]

Methodologically, continuous stratification of this form favours fitting several leading PCs as fixed covariates together with a kinship matrix as a random effect, rather than a single Q-matrix, to control false positives while preserving detection power [43]. The panel therefore sits at a productive point in the diversity–stratification trade-off: its allelic range is broad enough to power association detection, while its structure is correctable rather than confounding. Association signals recovered consistently across the panel are expected to be the most transferable across the ISRA–ICRISAT breeding continuum. Finally, the faster LD decay characteristic of West African pearl millet relative to South Asian material [12,36] means associations from Indian panels do not transfer directly to this context, reinforcing the value of a regionally anchored reference panel for future multi-trait and multi-environment GWAS in the Sahelian production system.

Linkage disequilibrium decayed rapidly, with mean r2 falling below 0.1 at approximately 8 kb across the 14,718 SNPs scored in the GWAS panel, consistent with the outcrossing biology of pearl millet, in which recurrent recombination erodes marker–marker correlations over short distances. The reference PMiGAP diversity panel reported even faster decay (r2 < 0.2 within 84–444 bp), a rate comparable to allogamous maize [11]. The greater LD extent observed here is expected from the panel’s composition: unlike a largely panmictic diversity set, our panel combined advanced inbred lines with locally derived breeding material, several entries sharing pedigree and subject to directional selection, both of which reduce effective recombination and extend haplotype blocks. Such subpopulation-dependent variation is documented in pearl millet, where the West-African subgroup shows greater decay owing to a longer recombination history [36]. The short-range LD confirms that dense, genome-wide marker coverage is required to capture causal variants [44].

Eleven MTAs were detected across six chromosomes for the traits under study, each association individually explaining a modest fraction of the overall phenotypic variance. This distribution is characteristic of the polygenic, small-effect architecture typical of quantitative agronomic traits in pearl millet, and it aligns with prior genome-wide work in the crop: the reference GWAS across test-cross progenies identified 1,054 significant MTAs for fifteen traits, with individual associations explaining between 9% and 27% of phenotypic variation [11]. The only exception in our study was on chromosome 4, where the marker SNPPM6939 associated with grain yield explained 48.67% of the phenotypic variance and had a negative effect on yield. An effect of this magnitude is atypical for a quantitative trait and should be interpreted with caution: in a panel of only 137 entries with no independent validation population, single-locus effect sizes are prone to substantial overestimation (the Beavis effect), and the value may partly reflect minor-allele frequency or allele-class imbalance rather than a true major effect. This need for independent confirmation is reinforced by the deleterious-variant burden documented in Senegalese pearl millet [45], which argues for building association resources on regionally adapted germplasm and validating candidate signals before they are deployed in selection.

Several of other associations correspond, at the chromosome level, to genomic regions previously implicated in the same traits. Earlier marker-based studies in pearl millet associated marker alleles with plant height on linkage group 7, and with panicle length on linkage groups 2, 5, and 7, while a further allele on linkage group 7 was associated with grain yield [44], and more recent association analyses have likewise recovered agronomic-trait associations for plant height, panicle length, and grain weight in the crop [46]. This convergence of independent panels and marker systems on broadly overlapping regions is consistent with these being genuine effects rather than artefacts; the correspondence is, however, at the chromosome level and does not by itself establish that the same underlying loci are involved.

A notable feature of the present results is that chromosome 4 harbored associations for three traits: grain yield (SNPPM6939, 3.9 Mb), plant height (SNPPM8294, 128.2 Mb), and panicle length (SNPPM8661, 227.9 Mb), making it, together with chromosome 2, the most trait-rich region in the panel. This co-occurrence does not, however, imply a shared genetic basis. The three markers are dispersed across more than 220 Mb of the chromosome, with the plant-height and panicle-length signals alone separated by roughly 100 Mb. Because linkage disequilibrium in this panel decayed to r2 < 0.1 within approximately 8 kb, associations this far apart cannot be in linkage with one another and instead represent physically independent loci that merely reside on the same chromosome. The co-localization of plant height and panicle-related traits reported previously in pearl millet [47] therefore does not extend to the present associations, which show no evidence of a single pleiotropic region governing multiple traits. The functional candidates underlying each of these independent signals are considered below. Inspection of the ± 8 kb intervals flanking the significant markers nominated several functionally credible candidates, which should be regarded as hypotheses for subsequent validation rather than confirmed causal genes. Because these candidates were identified solely by physical proximity to significant markers within LD-defined windows, their positions localize but do not establish a causal relationship, and the links proposed below are positional hypotheses to be tested functionally. Two gene families recurred in the intervals flanking the plant-architecture and panicle associations: F-box domain proteins and AP2/ERF transcription factors. The AP2/ERF family is a well-characterized regulator of inflorescence development and yield in cereals: in rice, these transcription factors participate in the regulation of panicle architecture, grain plumpness, and yield formation by controlling inflorescence meristem activity, cell division, and differentiation [48], and their agronomic relevance extends across grasses, in wheat, mutation of an AP2/ERF gene (DUO-B1) regulating spike architecture increased grain number per spike and raised field yield without penalizing other major agronomic traits [49]. The presence of an AP2/ERF candidate near the chromosome 4 region jointly associated with plant height and panicle length would therefore be consistent with a role in meristem determinacy and inflorescence patterning, though this remains to be demonstrated. The F-box candidates are similarly noteworthy: in rice, mutations in the F-box gene LARGER PANICLE improve panicle architecture and enhance grain yield [50], and non-synonymous variants in both an AP2/ERF gene and an F-box domain-containing protein were recently reported to jointly explain a large proportion of the variance for panicle exsertion [51]. The recurrence of these two families in our intervals parallels that functional pairing and supports their prioritization as candidates for follow-up, rather than confirming their involvement in the panicle-related associations.

For flowering time, the strongest a priori candidate in pearl millet is the phytochrome pathway. Natural variation at PHYTOCHROME C is a long-recognized determinant of phenology and morphology in the crop: association studies first linked natural variation at PHYC to flowering time and morphological variation across a set of inbred lines [41], a result subsequently refined through fine-scale association mapping and analysis of linkage disequilibrium and selection in the vicinity of the PHYTOCHROME C gene [52]. This locus has since been repeatedly implicated in Sahelian adaptation, having been identified as a major flowering-time gene underpinning selection for earlier flowering in response to climatic variation [31]; it is cited here as regional context, as the flowering association recovered in the present panel does not fall within the PHYC region. Flowering time is highly quantitative [53], so the single association recovered here most likely reflects the limited power of a panel of this size under a stringent multi-locus threshold, rather than a truly simple genetic basis, with a larger panel expected to resolve more loci. It is nonetheless tempting to speculate that crosstalk between photoreceptor and auxin-mediated pathways contributes to the phenological variation observed here, a hypothesis consistent with documented phytochrome–auxin interactions in other species [54] but one that would require direct functional testing to validate.

This study reported a genome-wide association analysis of grain yield, plant height, panicle length, and flowering time in a Senegalese pearl millet panel combining internationally derived inbred lines with locally adapted breeding material. Eleven MTAs were detected across six chromosomes, several linked to genes plausibly involved in cell expansion, inflorescence development, and hormone-mediated growth. Because associations from South Asian panels transfer poorly to West African germplasm, these results are of particular regional value, with the plant height and panicle length loci and the large-effect grain-yield locus on chromosome 4 emerging as the most robust and promising targets for marker-assisted and genomic selection. Realizing that potential will depend on functional validation of the candidate genes and confirmation of the associations in larger, stabilized panels spanning a wider range of West African environments. This case is reinforced by the burden of deleterious variants carried in Senegalese pearl millet germplasm, which argues both for confirming candidate signals on this genetic background and for using maturing genomic resources to track and progressively purge these alleles from the breeding pool while preserving its regional adaptation. Carried forward into multi-environment testing, genomic-selection pipelines, and regionally important constraints such as downy mildew and Striga, these findings offer a grounded basis for genomics-assisted pearl millet improvement in Senegal and the broader Sahel.

passages.text: In high-producing dairy cows, microbial composition can vary throughout the estrous cycle, in response to natural hormonal changes that affect pH, vaginal secretion profile, and local immunity. These physiological oscillations can modulate bacterial composition and diversity, resulting in specific microbial profiles for each phase of the cycle [2]. However, the use of hormonal protocols for estrus synchronization, a practice widely adopted in intensive production systems, can significantly interfere with this natural dynamic [3]. Interventions with progesterone, estrogens, prostaglandins, and gonadotropins alter the vaginal environment by modifying mucus, blood flow, and the immune response, potentially producing artificial changes in microbial composition. These alterations can mask or attenuate spontaneous variations in the microbiota, making it difficult to understand its natural behavior and its real influence on fertility [4,5].

In addition, the literature indicates that certain bacterial communities can serve as biomarkers of gestation in cattle, thereby complementing the interpretation of our results. More stable microbial profiles with lower abundance of opportunistic pathogens have been associated with higher conception rates, while subtle changes in groups such as Ureaplasma and some fermenting families (e.g., Ruminococcaceae) have been linked to better conditions for artificial insemination, especially when related to favorable hormone levels during estrus [7]. Taken together, these studies reinforce the idea that the presence of specific taxa during gestation or at critical moments of fertility may reflect physiological adjustments specific to reproduction, corroborating the notion that microbial biomarkers, although subtle, carry functional relevance and can distinguish physiological phases with greater precision than isolated diversity metrics [9,28].

Finally, the absence of marked differences between phases and the clear predominance of individual effects underscore the importance of investigating the determinants of the “ideal” or functional microbial composition of the reproductive tract. Longitudinal studies that track microbial changes before, during, and after conception, as well as integrated approaches combining metagenomics, metabolomics, and physiological parameters, can substantially deepen understanding of the microbiota-fertility interaction. The presence of several genera (e.g., Fibrobacter) that are not consistently reported in this niche was unexpected, and further studies are necessary to determine whether it is of fecal origin. This knowledge will be important not only to advance the reproductive management of high-producing dairy cows, but might also have implications for the intestinal colonization of calves.

passages.text: There has been a call for urgent action regarding climate change issues due to its threat to sustainable development worldwide [1,2]. Many renewable energy developers of wind and solar projects prefer to finance their work by issuing Green Bonds (GBs) rather than generating funds from traditional capital sources, such as equity or conventional debt. However, most of these projects are performing differently than expected due to the need for more financing. Despite the number of eco-friendly investments evolving worldwide, the climate challenge continues to progress, and the benefits of sustainable investments need to be more convincing in the market. Although GBs have appeared as a critical solution to persuade both energy producers and investors about the benefits of eco-friendly investments, the overly complicated GB frameworks and many other unidentified matters have hampered the development of the GB market [3,4]. Thus, linking renewable energy and the GB market would provide promising prospects for investors, developers, and sustainable development. However, the concept of GB needs to be appropriately defined and presented to market participants for the success of these prospects. Thus, this study aims to recognize the ways that could be used to scale up the GB market by identifying the stakeholders’ perceptions of the market.

Recent systematic reviews and empirical studies have substantially advanced understanding of Green Bond markets, pricing dynamics, and investor behaviour. [8] synthesize over 70 empirical pricing studies, reporting an average negative greenium of about −12.44 basis points while highlighting significant regional and methodological differences in pricing results. Other reviews also document modest but context-dependent yield discounts for Green Bonds relative to conventional bonds, noting liquidity, certification, and reporting standards as important moderators [9]. Empirical research further shows how macroeconomic conditions and investor composition shape greenium dynamics, with retail investor demand and bond credibility playing measurable roles [10]. The literature also emphasizes persistent concerns about greenwashing and information asymmetry, with empirical evidence from China showing that selective environmental disclosure can elevate credit spreads and undermine pricing credibility [11]. Finally, work on regulatory frameworks and environmental commitments highlights that uneven disclosure regimes and market standards materially influence pricing outcomes and investor confidence [12].

Studies on the GB market have further highlighted the defining issue in the GB market [2,13–17]. Investment in GB carries the risk of greenwashing, as there is no proper mechanism for investors to ensure the appropriate use of the proceeds of their investments [17]. Moreover, the increasing number of green certificate providers in the GB market is giving rise to a so-called regulatory environment—one that is shaped by market practices rather than formal oversight—despite the absence of a proper legal framework, a governing body to monitor the market, or a commonly accepted definition of what constitutes a green certificate. According to [17], certificate providers aim to align the preferences of investors intending to participate in the Green Bond market with established green criteria, thereby enabling asset managers to implement those preferences efficiently. Local governments should focus on finding ways to give greater importance to environmental impacts in rating and certification systems by offering financial incentives and low-carbon subsidies [18].

Apart from different definitions, there are several instruments to measure the ‘greenness’ of projects, such as second opinions, green ratings, and GB indices, which are not consistent in terms of the degree of the scale, the availability of ex-post monitoring, and the availability of quantitative tools [19]. Hence, determining the true environmental impact—or “greenness”—of projects remains challenging, which in turn undermines credibility in the GB market and reduces investor confidence [20]. As argued in [21], many Green Bonds lack binding legal commitments to ensure that funds are directed toward environmental objectives. They highlight the disconnect between the marketed environmental promises and the actual legal structure of Green Bonds, which often mirrors that of conventional debt instruments. This accountability gap raises concerns about greenwashing, where issuers may overstate or misrepresent the environmental benefits of their bonds without significant legal or reputational consequences.

As the Green Bond market continues to evolve, research should focus on its role in reshaping financial markets and fostering economic sustainability [25]. Thus, it is essential to identify how stakeholders perceive the market and what will provide assurance for investors and regulators regarding the green claims of corporate bond issuers [15]. Despite significant advances in understanding greenium dynamics, investor behavior, regulatory frameworks, and risks such as greenwashing, gaps remain in integrating these findings into cohesive conceptual models of market behaviour. Our study addresses these gaps by synthesising institutional barriers, stakeholder interpretations, and qualitative insights that complement existing quantitative research. The study’s main analysis is based on global publications, supplemented by interviews from the Australian and European markets. We suggest mechanisms to upscale the GB market to meet annual green investment needs worldwide, along with a theoretical framework that explains the relationship between stakeholder perception and scaling up the GB market.

In reference to GBs, the same problem prevails, as different economic and policy areas identify ‘greenness’ differently. Experts in the GB market stress that GB market growth is ‘strangled’ because of the presence of less-harmonised bond frameworks [3]. Climate Bonds Initiative and the International Capital Markets Association act as the central regulatory bodies for GB issues. While the ICMA defines GBs in line with the GBPs, the CBI issues a certificate for greenness to label a bond as a GB. The ICMA provided the same definition in the GBPs issued from 2014 to 2021, yet changes were made to the list of eligible green projects. The GBPs of the ICMA do not broadly discuss ‘greenness’ but provide broader categories of eligible green projects. The GBPs illustrate that new areas are introduced as ‘green’ each year. As the secretary to the GBPs, the [36] defines a GB as:

In other words, a bond is a GB if the issuer uses the proceeds of the issue totally for capital expenditures for green or climate-related environmental benefits [37] and follows all four GBPs. The two critical aspects emphasised by this definition are financing and traceability, which are vital to the development of the GB market. GBs that provide investors with access to the market for information on ongoing projects that meet the green standards grant some assurance to investors through traceability and reporting requirements [38]. However, the [39] criticised the space provided to re-label a Conventional Bond (CB) as a GB through this definition. It argued that this might provide an incentive to ‘greenwash’. Greenwashing is identified as giving the impression of changing a project to have environmental benefits, while not actually making this change [19]. However, Urik Ross, the global head of public sector and sustainable finance at HSBC, stated that:

However, there are no sector-specific or common criteria to assess the compliance of projects with GBPs, and the issuer is entitled to label their projects as green upon the issuance of GBs. Nevertheless, to enhance the credibility of the issue, issuers can obtain a green label through the CBI. To assess the ‘greenness’ of projects, the CBI can assess its compliance with the GBPs using the CBS. However, the criteria to assess greenness under the CBS are currently only available on projects categorised as solar energy, wind energy, geothermal energy, low-carbon transport or low-carbon building [41]. The CBS does not define GBs; however, if a GB meets the requirements of the CBS, it can be identified as a certified climate bond.

However, this definition is only used in the interbank market, and has subsequently been criticised as a local definition that cannot be applied to international bond issues or to local issues by any other sector [48]. The 2016 China GB Market report issued by the CBI emphasised that this definition and the projects it identifies as green are not consistent with international standards, and are not considered by international investors. Moreover, the project categories and process for issuing a GB according to the PBoC guidelines and NDRC regulations are also not synchronised. However, these guidelines have attracted a significant investor base as mandatory requirements. As a result, China became the largest GB market in the world in 2017 [49] and was second in 2018 [50].

All definitions discussed above emphasise that the type of investment or project should be climate-related, environmental or ‘green’. The issuer of the bond uses different definitions of GB to suit their requirements and business profile [15,43]. However, to enable high reliance in the market, it is essential to avoid different interpretations of what is meant by ‘green’ [15]. Furthermore, it is evident that great efforts have already been invested by different institutions to define ‘green’ in relation to GBs. However, none of these definitions are able to precisely quantify the green measurement criteria in their definitions, except for Moody’s GBA methodology. When explaining the need to ensure straightforward and clearer guidelines in the GB market, Sean Kidney stressed that regulators should clarify the projects eligible to be labelled as green, thereby enabling investors to assess the positive effects of their investments:

Accordingly, investors expected further criteria to minimise greenwashing concerns and increase the credibility of a GB issue. They believed that the project categories identified by the GBPs to be climate and environmentally friendly. However, issuers were expected to compare their targeted environmental impacts with publicly available criteria to improve the credibility of a particular issue. Moreover, the investors required additional due diligence reports from projects that offer only marginal benefits to the environment, despite being originally categorised as ‘green’, such as large-scale hydro and nuclear power generation, and greenhouse gas reductions from coal-fired power plants. Further, for projects that are not originally environment and climate focused, investors require a substantial contribution to the sustainable management of eco-resources, plans to reduce waste or pollution, and enhancements to environmental quality.

Opinions of GB issuers and regulators in the market at the Asia Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association (ASIFMA) Green Finance Conference, organised by the United Nations Climate Change Secretariat and United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific in July 2018, are quoted by [3]. Sean Kidney expressed his view on the unnecessary requirements in some reporting frameworks, which complicate the issuing procedure. He stated that it is not necessary to implement compulsory reporting on greenhouse gas emissions for solar energy projects, while showing the necessity of reporting this measure by geothermal projects. He explained that it is necessary to minimise the work of the issuance, while maximising the work of the wider framework in which GBs are issued.

In the IISD report [15], suggested three major barriers in the GB market: (1) lower market credibility because of the absence of a clear definition, (2) lower project transparency and (3) liquidity and risk/return constraints. According to the IISD report, the GB market has a significant potential institutional investor base who are seeking clear green features for investments towards sustainability goals. Two hundred and fifty-nine institutional investors who possess a combined US$29 trillion in assets contributed to the global investor coalition on climate change. Although they have the intention to contribute to a low-carbon economy, the absence of transparent green claims prevents their investment. Furthermore, lower market liquidity due to the lack of large-sized GB issues and low credit ratings also poses a challenge in the market. In relation to zero-emission renewable energy projects, less than 50% from the total outstanding GBs achieved investment grade.

The consultation report issued by the [60] in 2015 identified the prevailing problems under five themes: (1) challenges to market development, (2) challenges to increasing GB issuance, (3) challenges to enabling a wider range of issuers and projects, (4) challenges to increasing GB investments and (5) challenges to increasing cooperation in scaling the GB market. First, the absence of clear standards and guidance was identified as the main problem preventing GB market growth. The report emphasised the need to implement well-established green credentials in the GB market to achieve climate goals worldwide. It argued that the problem of using GB proceeds to finance projects with little environmental benefits—and claiming these projects to be green (greenwashing)—can only be mitigated through sound standards and policies. Second, limited bankable green projects and reduced awareness among potential green project owners about the benefits of financing these projects through GBs are highlighted as the main challenges to increasing the supply side of the market. Lack of awareness is a problem mainly in emerging economies, as evidenced by the current list of GB issuers, who largely represent developed economies.

Third, bond diversity and scale were identified as major factors to be considered in GB market development, as greater scale and diversity will help attract more issuers and investors to the market. Therefore, small-scale projects, lack of aggregation mechanisms and low credit ratings were introduced as the major challenges to enabling a wider range of issuers and projects. Fourth, the report identified capacity constraints because of a lack of publicly available historical data, lower availability of credit ratings and reduced awareness of investors as challenges to increasing GB investments. Finally, lower harmonisation and cooperation between key market participants were identified as the main challenges to overcome. Overall, government intervention was highly recommended by the CBI [60] as a remedy to the identified key barriers. The report suggested some recommendations/policy actions to be taken by the public sector, which are discussed under Theme 04 of this study.

To improve trustworthiness, it is essential to verify the greenness of projects and to continuously monitor and report the use of proceeds. However, at this stage, there is no commonly accepted definition, standard or methodology for this assessment and reporting; thus, potential issuers must seek professional services from external reviewers for pre- and post-audits. According to [16], the professional service fee can range from US$10,000 to US$100,000 per annum. Additionally, issuers must spend significant amounts on periodic reporting requirements. This high cost discourages potential issuers from issuing large GB issues to the market. Literature reports size of the issue as a key factor for bond investments [20,62,63]. Therefore, without large GB issues, investors may be discouraged from making GB investments.

If the issuer does not demonstrate reliable green credentials through their GB prospectus or issuing framework, investors must obtain a second opinion before making the investment. This creates a high transaction cost for investors and restricts investment decisions. When explaining the reasons for the high cost associated with second-party reviews, [16] focused their attention on three key factors. First, because there is no standardised methodology for the majority of second-opinion providers, reviews can vary, even within the same provider. This causes investors to obtain separate reviews on green credentials for each GB issue, even if the issues are made by the same issuer. Second, the opinion can be biased. Most second-party opinion providers are involved in the preparation of GB frameworks by issuers and the review of the same for investors. Third, reviews generally do not provide disclosures on the environmental impact of the bond. Moreover, reviewers do not monitor the use of proceeds throughout the bond term and do not undertake the liability for the project’s validation.

This study was motivated by several issues identified in the GB market. First, the GB market development was identified as essential as a new source of financing for ‘green’ projects. This was evident by the CBI’s CEO statement that GBs are ‘the Trojan horse’ of sustainable financing. However, the market is not at the scale needed to meet worldwide green finances. Different stakeholders characterise the GB market. Therefore, identifying the ‘greenness’ of a project financed by GBs is problematic. The low credibility of the GB issuance process is highly questioned by potential investors, who express concern regarding the possibility of greenwashing. Therefore, an in-depth study of the GB market is timely to identify the reasons for the limitations in this market. Second, while prior studies have substantially advanced understanding of Green Bond pricing, investor behaviour, and market performance, relatively limited attention has been given to integrating global policy frameworks with stakeholder perceptions into a unified conceptual explanation of barriers to scaling the Green Bond market. This study addresses that gap by synthesising documentary evidence with exploratory stakeholder insights. A better understanding of the market will help researchers build new theories of the GB market and suggest improved practices and recommendations.

The integrated framework demonstrates that the challenges of definitional ambiguity can be interpreted from three complementary theoretical perspectives. Stakeholder theory explains how divergent expectations among issuers, investors and regulators create competing interpretations of “greenness.” Institutional theory highlights how fragmented regulatory systems and evolving norms prevent convergence towards common market standards. Market failure theory explains how information asymmetry and negative externalities reduce investor confidence and weaken incentives for market participation. Together, these perspectives provide a richer explanation of why persistent structural barriers continue to constrain the scaling of the GB market beyond what any individual theory can explain independently. Further, the model demonstrates that scaling the Green Bond market depends not solely on financial performance, but on coordinated stakeholder alignment supported by effective policy mechanisms.

Our study is based on qualitative analysis of selected institutional documents and five expert interviews, primarily representing developed-market perspectives. While triangulation enhances internal validity, the findings should not be interpreted as statistically generalizable. Instead, they provide analytically grounded insights into structural barriers and stakeholder perceptions within the GB market. Future research may employ large-scale surveys or cross-country qualitative designs to further validate and extend these findings. Furthermore, another key limitation concerns the geographically concentrated interview sample. Although documentary evidence reflects global developments, stakeholder interviews were conducted primarily within the Australian and European markets. Future research should extend qualitative inquiry to emerging markets and diverse institutional contexts to enhance comparative generalizability. Given the rapid evolution of sustainable finance frameworks after 2021, including the expansion of green taxonomies and post-pandemic recovery instruments, stakeholder perceptions may have evolved. Longitudinal qualitative research would provide valuable insights into how these perceptions have shifted over time.

passages.text: Blockchain technology has revolutionized the structure of financial systems by enabling decentralized, trustless transactions through distributed ledgers. The rapid growth in cryptocurrencies has significantly reshaped the global financial landscape. Since the launch of Bitcoin in 2009 [1], the number of cryptocurrencies has expanded dramatically [2–5]. As of April 2025, there are approximately 25,000 active cryptocurrencies, including both coins and tokens across various blockchain platforms. Together, they hold a total market capitalization of around USD 2.96 trillion [6]. Cryptocurrencies have gained widespread attention due to their decentralized nature, lower transaction costs compared to traditional fiat currencies, and the transparency they offer [7–9]. At the core of cryptocurrencies lies blockchain technology, a distributed append-only ledger that securely records transactions [9,10]. Blockchains often operate with native cryptocurrencies, which can be traded for traditional money through exchanges like Binance [11]. The ability to freely exchange cryptocurrencies has significantly fueled their market growth. It has also enabled new fundraising methods, such as Initial Coin Offerings (ICOs), where blockchain-based digital tokens are sold directly to participants [12,13].

Among various blockchain platforms, Ethereum has emerged as a dominant platform, supporting programmable smart contracts and the proliferation of ERC20 tokens that underpin a wide range of decentralized financial applications [12]. To facilitate token development and exchange, the Ethereum community introduced the ERC20 token standard in November 2015 [14]. Although it is not mandatory, the ERC20 standard has been adopted widely, with the majority of Ethereum-based tokens being ERC20 compatible [13]. One of the unique features of Ethereum is its dual-account model, consisting of Externally Owned Accounts (EOAs), which are controlled by private keys [12], and smart contracts (SCs), which are autonomous programs executing predefined logic [15,16]. This structure creates two different types of interactions on the Ethereum network: externally initiated (EOA-driven) and SC-driven (contract-based) transactions. These distinct modes of operation give rise to heterogeneous behavioral patterns across the network. As the volume and complexity of blockchain activity continue to grow, understanding the underlying transactional dynamics, particularly the differences between EOA-driven and SC-driven, becomes increasingly essential for ensuring transparency.

Several studies have explored ERC20 token transactions from various angles. For instance, Victor et al. [8] analyzed the wash trading activity on decentralized exchanges like IDEX and EtherDelta and found that over 30% of the tokens traded were involved in wash trading, indicating manipulative behavior. Pradeep et al. [17] examined the behavior of ERC20 token traders during the 2018 crypto crash and the COVID-19 pandemic, revealing that trader interactions became more diverse in response to these market shocks, reflecting increased adoption of ERC20 tokens. Chen et al. [12] investigated the broader ERC20 ecosystem, raising important concerns about market manipulation and token price dynamics. In addition, Victor et al. [13] identified hub-and-spoke patterns in token transaction networks and observed that many tokens were primarily sold rather than circulated, highlighting imbalances in token flow. While these studies provide valuable insights into the ERC20 ecosystem, they generally treat token transactions as a unified whole, without explicitly differentiating between EOA-based and SC-based interactions. However, such a distinction is crucial for understanding how EOAs and SCs operate differently, which could unveil deeper structural and behavioral patterns in token transactions. Despite the dual-account model of Ethereum being central to its design, there remains a significant research gap in developing robust frameworks that systematically distinguish between these account types to better interpret the heterogeneous dynamics of ERC20 token activity.

Earlier blockchain studies have identified power-law patterns in transaction networks, reflecting scalable and heterogeneous interactions [18–20]. Somin et al. [19] demonstrated that transaction volumes in ERC20 networks follow power-law distributions, akin to those observed in social [21] and biological networks [22]. Wu et al. [20] further showed that the market capitalizations of coins and tokens also exhibit power-law behavior. While power laws describe scalable transaction patterns, another canonical scaling law, Taylor’s law (TL), measures fluctuation stability. Originally introduced to describe the relationship between the mean and variance of population sizes in ecological systems [23], TL has since been applied across a range of domains. In particular, it has gained prominence in economic and financial contexts as a tool for quantifying volatility and dynamic fluctuations in market activity [24,25]. Despite the relevance of both scaling laws, no prior study has combined these frameworks to dissect the behavioral signatures of EOA-driven and SC–driven interactions in blockchain ecosystems. Our study bridges this gap by integrating power-law analysis with TL to investigate ERC20 token transactions. While power-law exponents help reveal whether transactional dynamics are dominated by different account types, Taylor’s law provides insight into the stability of these interactions over time. Together, these methods offer a unified framework for distinguishing behavioral modes in decentralized systems, enabling a more granular understanding of ERC20 transaction types.

To address this research gap, we classify ERC20 transactions into four distinct categories based on the nature of interaction: EOA–EOA, EOA–SC, SC–EOA, and SC–SC. We investigate whether consistent statistical regularities—such as power-law scaling and fluctuation relationships—emerge across these interaction types. Specifically, we analyze the scaling relationship between trade volume and partner diversity, fit power-law models to transaction distributions, and apply TL to assess the stability and persistence of scaling behavior over time. Our findings uncover clear statistical contrasts between EOA-driven and SC–driven activities in ERC20 transactions, offering deeper insights into the operational dynamics of decentralized financial systems. Beyond categorizing transactional roles, this study emphasizes how decentralized finance (DeFi) ecosystems are shaped by the interplay of EOA-driven decisions and SC-driven executions. As DeFi platforms increasingly rely on smart contracts for lending, trading, and asset management, understanding different account-type interaction patterns, EOA–EOA, EOA–SC, and SC–SC, is crucial for interpreting their impact on market stability, liquidity dynamics, and the emergence of complex behaviors in blockchain-based economies.

We analyzed ERC20 token transactions on the Ethereum blockchain by categorizing interactions into four types—EOA–EOA, EOA–SC, SC–EOA, and SC–SC—according to whether the sender and receiver accounts were EOAs or smart contracts. The central goal was to determine whether these interaction types exhibit consistent and statistical signatures over time. Our results show that EOA-driven transactions display highly regular, scalable, and predictable behavior, as evidenced by near-linear scaling relationships, robust power-law distributions with heavy tails, and stable TL exponents across all periods analyzed. These findings indicate that EOA-driven blockchain transactions follow statistical patterns observed in traditional economic and social systems. In contrast, SC-driven interactions, particularly SC–SC exchanges, exhibited greater variability, characterized by sublinear scaling, unstable and threshold-sensitive power-law exponents, and frequent deviations from theoretical models. These irregularities were further reflected in elevated KS distances and larger standard errors. These patterns suggest that smart contract behavior is not governed by uniform dynamics but is instead shaped by contextual factors such as protocol design, automation logic, and transaction purpose.

Overall, our findings uncover statistically distinctive features of EOA versus SC-driven interactions on the ERC20 network. While EOA-driven transactions align with established behavioral laws observed in traditional economic and social systems, SC interactions tend to be more context-dependent and structurally volatile. A gas fee analysis further supports this distinction, showing that EOA–SC transactions consistently incur approximately 3 times higher gas fees than EOA–EOA transactions across all periods, consistent with the greater computational complexity of smart contract execution, while also reflecting gas-price and fee-market dynamics. This distinction highlights the importance of adopting separate analytical frameworks for modeling EOA-driven and SC-driven behavior in decentralized systems. These insights are not only critical for designing resilient DeFi infrastructures but also offer valuable indicators for monitoring systemic risk and volatility in emerging crypto-financial markets.

In future work, we plan to extend this framework across multiple blockchain platforms (e.g., Binance Smart Chain, Solana, Avalanche) to evaluate whether similar statistical patterns persist beyond Ethereum. Moreover, exploring causal mechanisms behind smart contract volatility, such as governance rules, transaction fee dynamics, or oracle dependencies, can offer deeper insights into protocol-level fragilities. Subsequent studies will incorporate sensitivity analyses that exclude known airdrop and exchange flows, stratify smart contract interactions by contract type, and extend the analysis to include graph topological features such as clustering coefficient, modularity, and node centrality to provide a more complete structural characterization of ERC20 transaction networks. Lastly, integrating machine learning techniques to classify behavioral regimes and anomalies at scale will open the path toward intelligent monitoring of DeFi ecosystems.

passages.text: Identifying the ecological mechanisms that determine which species persist in anthropogenic mosaics remains a critical challenge. Niche research has traditionally focused on its position, understood as the environmental optima or “average” preferences of a species, to predict response to habitat modification [11,12]. However, niche position alone often fails to account for the complexity of human-disturbed landscapes. Urbanized and agricultural landscapes often combine environmental conditions (e.g., temperature, vegetation structure, soil characteristics, and resource availability) in ways that species may not have previously experienced [13]. In contrast to the relative stability of natural environments, human-modified landscapes are often highly fragmented, constantly fluctuating, and perturbed [14,15]. Recent studies increasingly recognize niche breadth as an important determinant of species persistence under environmental change because it defines the range of abiotic conditions and biotic resources that species can tolerate and exploit [16–21]. Broader niche breadth is generally associated with greater ecological generalism, whereas a narrower niche breadth is associated with greater ecological specialization [19,22]. Consequently, species with relatively narrow niche breadths are expected to be more vulnerable to the environmental filtering associated with land use change [9,18]. On the other hand, broader niche breadth may facilitate species persistence by enabling more tolerance across novel combinations of environmental conditions [18,19].

The greater persistence of species with broader realized niche breadths in human-modified landscapes has been documented across a wide range of taxa [9,18,19]. For instance, avian generalists are more likely to maintain stable populations in urban centres than specialists [23–25]. Similar patterns have been observed in rodents, bats, reptiles, amphibians, and insects, where a positive relationship exists between niche breadth and occupancy in landscapes altered by humans [26,27]. Recent work on butterflies further supports this pattern, showing that species with broader environmental niches are more likely to persist across agricultural landscapes than habitat specialists [28]. However, many previous studies infer niche breadth from species’ presence–absence records or broad habitat categories, providing limited insight into how fine-scale environmental gradients shape realized niche breadth and species persistence [19,28,29]. Consequently, whether differences in realized niche breadth measured across fine-scale environmental gradients explain the contrasting persistence of ecosystem engineers in human-modified landscapes remains largely unknown. Ecosystem engineers are taxa that physically modify their environment [30,31]. Understanding how they respond to novel environmental conditions arising from rapid land-use change is therefore critical, as their persistence or exclusion can have cascading effects on soil structure, nutrient cycling, and ecosystem functioning [32,33].

Beyond the environmental gradients that we evaluated here, predation may also contribute to the contrasting persistence of both species in human-modified landscapes. Leaf-cutting ants are attacked by a variety of natural enemies, including phorid flies, armadillos, beetles, birds, and spiders, which can influence colony establishment, foraging activity, and colony survival [74,75]. However, little is known about whether changes in predator communities across forests, pastures, and urban environments differentially affect A. cephalotes and A. laevigata. An additional anthropogenic pressure may arise from the traditional harvest of reproductive females of A. laevigata for human consumption in the Santander region, whereas comparable exploitation of A. cephalotes is disproportionately lower [76]. Since the demographic consequences of this harvest remain unknown, both natural predation and human harvesting deserve further attention as potential ecological filters acting alongside realized niche breadth in shaping species persistence under land-use change.

We also identified several methodological aspects that deserve further attention. First, some sampling locations contained substantially more colonies of one species than the other because of their natural distribution across the landscape. Future designs should aim for a more homogeneous species distribution across sites to control for potential site-specific biases. Second, while we maintained a minimum distance of 100 meters between colonies to ensure independence, the future integration of precise GPS coordinates would allow for a more granular analysis of micro-climatic gradients and spatial autocorrelation [38,39]. Third, although the variables that we selected for this study (pH, canopy openness, and mound architecture) captured key dimensions of the realized niche, they represent only a subset of a multivariate space [12]. To further refine our understanding of niche breadth, future research should incorporate additional environmental and biological axes, such as soil moisture, mound entrance dimensions, and specific foraging preferences. Fourth, our inference that differences in realized niche breadth contribute to contrasting persistence in human-modified landscapes is based on direct measurements of niche breadth combined with previously reported presence of A. cephalotes in urban areas. Future studies should evaluate colony survival, growth, and persistence across human-modified environments within the same study area to directly test this hypothesis. Finally, as these ecosystem engineers exist in an obligate symbiosis with the fungus L. gongylophorus [34,36], focusing solely on the ant provides an incomplete picture. Because colony performance depends on both partners, future work should evaluate how the responses of both the ants and L. gongylophorus to environmental conditions contribute to differences in realized niche breadth.

Land-use change in the Anthropocene is reshaping species distributions across natural and human-modified landscapes [15]. As our analyses suggest, agropastoral expansion could favour the open-canopy specialist A. laevigata, while simultaneously displacing A. cephalotes from its typical woody habitats. This shift involves more than species turnover; it may alter nutrient cycling and other ecosystem processes within shaded forest patches. While A. cephalotes nests are known to create localized nutrient-depleted zones [32] and significantly elevate CO2 emissions [82], they also drive essential forest heterogeneity by altering canopy structure and light infiltration [65]. The decline of this engineer may trigger ecological cascades in forest remnants [36,39]. At the same time, the increasing occurrence of A. cephalotes in urban environments and the expansion of A. laevigata across agricultural landscapes may increase the frequency of human–ant interactions, potentially amplifying their impact as pests [42,55]. Understanding the environmental filters associated with land-use change is therefore important for improving the management of human-modified landscapes by helping predict where A. laevigata is likely to expand and where A. cephalotes may increase occurrence in urban areas.

We investigated whether the leaf-cutter ants A. cephalotes and A. laevigata in an area of the Colombian Andes differed in realized niche breadth across fine-scale environmental gradients, and whether those patterns are consistent with ecological strategies of generalism and specialization. Such strategies may shape species response to the ecological filter of ongoing land-use change. A. cephalotes presented a broader niche breadth for canopy openness and soil pH, along with a high association with woody-type vegetation. In contrast, A. laevigata showed a narrower niche for these environmental variables and an affinity for grasses in open areas, with a larger heat buffering capacity. Mound architecture characterization revealed a comparable elliptical shape, while mounds of A. laevigata were significantly larger than those of A. cephalotes. Our results support the hypothesis of generalism in A. cephalotes capable of occupying a broader range of microhabitats at local and regional scale, while also suggesting specialization of A. laevigata, better suited for cleared agro-pastoral landscapes. The findings suggest that a broader realized niche breadth is consistent with the documented occurrence of A. cephalotes in urban areas. This study contributes to the understanding of species responses to the ecological filter created by land-use change in view of the growing demand for agricultural lands and may support the management of human-modified landscapes.
